Chapter 8. The Practice of Gratitude: Finding Light in the Ordinary.
You know, when life’s filled with loss and disappointment, gratitude can feel like a language you just don’t speak. But for this family, learning to spot the good—even the tiniest bit of it—became a real lifeline.
It all started with a really simple habit: every night before bed, each person would name just one thing they were grateful for.
In the beginning, the list felt short. Maybe it was a warm meal, a kind word, or just a moment of peace. But as days went by, something interesting happened—they started noticing more. The way sunlight danced through the window. The sound of laughter, even if it only lasted a second. The comfort of a favorite song on a tough day.
Then, one morning after a restless night, a child pointed out a rainbow stretching across the sky. And just for a moment, the heaviness lifted—replaced by a sense of wonder. That’s when it really sank in: gratitude isn’t about pretending pain doesn’t exist. It’s about making room for a little joy, even when you’re hurting.
Most of us wait for something big before we feel grateful. But this family discovered that the ordinary is packed with gifts, if you’re looking for them. Just saying these things out loud—or jotting them down in a journal—helped shift their focus. Sure, the problems didn’t magically disappear, but they stopped defining every single moment.
Of course, there were days when gratitude seemed impossible. Days when the pain was too sharp, or the loss felt too heavy. On those days, the family let themselves grieve. But even then, they tried to find one small thing to hold onto. And over time, this simple practice became a source of resilience.
Gratitude didn’t change what they were going through, but it changed how they moved through it. They started showing up for each other, feeling more hopeful, and finding beauty—even in the midst of brokenness.
What really matters is this: gratitude isn’t just something you feel. It’s something you do—a way of choosing light, even when the world feels dark.
